opening.headline: We address the invisible issue of where LLM calls slow down by examining signal and context propagation, as well as GenAI property specifications.
body: Suppose a single user request takes 9 seconds to go through the gateway, search, LLM call, and post-processing before reaching a response. In the logs, the statements from each service are scattered, and the average latency graph only indicates that the process is slow, without revealing which specific phase is causing the delay.

In this class, we distinguish what logs, metrics, and traces answer respectively, and examine context propagation that links signals across different services within a single request. We then read the GenAI semantic conventions defining which properties should be included in LLM call spans, and diagnose trace discontinuity by examining headers.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain OpenTelemetry signals and context propagation
The properties of GenAI semantic constraints can explain what kind of questions they answer.
The cause of a broken trace can be analyzed by reading and examining header and span information.

screens.title: I don't see where the LLM call is slowing down
screens.lead: First, let's examine the scene where it's unclear what to check when the response becomes slow. Read through it while considering whether you can determine the time taken for each section of the diagram.

visual.alt: The request passes through the gateway, search, LLM call, and post-processing sequentially, and responds within 9 seconds.
labels: Only the fact of slowness is shown

paragraphs: A single user request takes 9 seconds to go through the gateway, search, LLM call, and post-processing before returning a response—a significantly slower response than usual. We need to determine where the time is being spent in order to fix it.

However, the logs contain fragmented messages per service, making it difficult to trace and follow the record of a single request. The average latency graph only indicates that latency is high, without providing the underlying reasons. There is no linkage showing how long each interval took or which model was used for the LLM call.

Observability is the property that allows us to understand why something happens simply by observing the signals that emerge from the system without needing to peek inside its internal workings. This course sequentially covers the types of signals, context propagation that links signals into a single request, and common conventions for LLM call properties.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The fact that something is slow is different from where it is slow. By the end of class, you will be able to distinguish which signal answers which question.

screens.outro: First, let's recall the differences between three signals.

screens.title: Can you explain the differences between logs, metrics, and traces?
screens.lead: When you select a card, the instructor's thought summary is displayed. Since you haven't entered an answer yet, first recall which question each signal responds to, then click it.

items.answer: A log is a sentence that records an event. For example, it indicates that a login failure occurred at a specific time, thereby informing us of what happened and when. An event can be viewed as a special type of log. While it provides detailed information about a single event, it does not display the complete path of the request.

items.prompt: What does a metric tell us?
items.answer: Metrics are measurements captured at runtime, such as aggregated values over a specific period like error rates, CPU utilization, or request rates. They provide an overview of whether the service is generally performing well or if errors are increasing. However, it is difficult to determine why a particular request is slow based solely on numerical data.

Trace shows the path a request took as it passed through an application. It displays which services were invoked and how long each segment took. To know the time breakdown of a request that took nine seconds, you need a trace.

screens.outro: Now that we recall the roles of the three signals, let's compare how the same request appears in each signal.

screens.title: Signal: Trace, Metric, Log, and Measurement
screens.lead: Select each tab to verify how the same 9-second request appears across each signal. In the last tab, you'll explore the measurement process that generates the signals.

tabs.label: trace
tabs.body: Trace shows the path a request takes through the application. For a nine-second request, components such as gateway, search, LLM call, and post-processing are displayed side by side, allowing you to immediately see which segment took longer. If the LLM call segment takes seven seconds, the location of the issue is immediately apparent.

tabs.label: metric
tabs.body: Metrics are measurements captured at runtime, such as error rates, CPU utilization, and request rates, which are aggregated over a specific period. A single request is represented by only one point in the latency distribution. While suitable for trends and alerts, they do not capture the full path of individual requests.

tabs.label: log
tabs.body: Logs record events. For the same request, each service is represented by individual lines. Containing timestamps, service names, and messages, they provide detailed information about the event; however, without information that groups logs from different services within the same request, it becomes difficult to follow the sequence.

tabs.label: Baggage
tabs.body: Baggage is contextual information transmitted between signals. It is used to establish that signals originate from the same request. However, sensitive information such as user authentication credentials, API keys, or personal data should not be included in baggage. Baggage is transmitted across service boundaries for this reason.

tabs.label: Measurement
tabs.body: The purpose of OpenTelemetry is to collect, process, and export telemetry data. Instrumenting an application refers to adding code so that it can export telemetry data. By pre-instrumenting with the necessary information, you can identify the root cause of issues without having to add additional code when a failure occurs. Furthermore, since a service may produce incorrect results even while running, reliability should be judged based on whether the service behaves as expected by users.

screens.outro: Let's examine what is required for traces to span across service boundaries.

screens.title: Context propagation and Trace Context
screens.lead: Select the following arrow to step through and see how the context is passed when service A calls service B.

visual.alt: Service A calls Service B by attaching a traceparent header, with B's span treating A's span as its parent.
labels: A's span (trace ID: same value, span ID: parent)
B's new span (same trace ID, parent-id = A's span ID)

steps.title: What is context?
steps.body: Context is an object containing the information necessary to connect one signal to another signal. The core information consists of trace ID and span ID. With context, signals generated in different services can be grouped together as part of the same request.

steps.title: Service A sends the context.
steps.body: When service A calls service B, it sends the trace ID and span ID as part of the context. If it's an HTTP call, these values are included in the request header. The span ID from service A becomes the parent information for service B.

steps.title: Service B creates a child span.
steps.body: Service B creates a new span within the same trace using the received value, with A's span as its parent. Therefore, the entire flow can be followed within a single trace even though the request crosses service boundaries.

steps.title: Radio waves are serializing and deserializing.
steps.body: Propagation is a mechanism for transferring context between services and processes. The context object is serialized and sent, and the receiving side deserializes it to retrieve the context. Typically, a telemetry library handles this process on behalf of the user, making it invisible to them. When direct propagation is required, the Propagators API should be used.

steps.title: The foundation is W3C Trace Context
steps.body: OpenTelemetry's default propagation mechanism uses HTTP headers defined by the W3C Trace Context specification. The `traceparent` header represents the position of a request within a trace graph in a fixed-length format, while the `tracestate` header adds vendor-specific information.

steps.title: The responsibilities of the intermediate system
steps.body: A system located in between, such as a proxy or gateway, must at minimum forward `traceparent` and `tracestate` unchanged. Only then will the trace remain intact. Optionally, header values can be modified to participate in the trace, but forwarding itself is the minimum requirement.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the structure of the signal, we will now examine the agreement regarding what to include in the LLM call span.

screens.title: GenAI Semantic Constraints: Attributes of LLM Call Span
screens.lead: When you hover over or select the terms highlighted below, a brief description appears. Review each term sequentially to understand why the agreement is necessary.

visual.alt: One LLM call span box and a diagram next to it with a list of attribute labels attached.
labels: What kind of task is this?

data.text: GenAI Semantic Protocol defines spans, metrics, events, MCP, and provider-specific conventions for GenAI clients, such as OpenAI. These conventions are managed in a separate repository that extends the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions. The need for these conventions arises because, regardless of the provider or framework used, If the property name is common then enables consistent comparison of models and usage under the same naming scheme. The type of operation is represented as a gen_ai.operation.name attribute, where "chat" is used for model conversation calls and "execute_tool" for tool executions. span name combines the operation and model into a format such as "chat model name." By preserving model names along with input and output Token count and error information as attributes, slow segments and expensive calls can be directly identified within traces. Backend services like Datadog interpret spans adhering to these conventions as LLM traces.

terms.tip: This is an OpenTelemetry specification that unifies the attribute names and meanings used in LLM call spans, metrics, and events.

terms.term: If the property name is common then
terms.tip: Even if the provider differs, it is recorded under the same name, meaning that model-specific usage and latency can be compared on a single screen.
This attribute indicates the type of operation being performed. Model conversation calls are represented as "chat", while tool executions are represented as "execute_tool".
This is the name of a call within a trace section. If you include both the task and the model, you can determine what call it is just by looking at the list.
The number of tokens used for input and output. This serves as a clue for estimating call costs and latency.

screens.outro: Now let's directly examine the header and span code.

screens.title: Reading header and span code: traceparent and gen_ai attributes
screens.lead: Read the header and code below from top to bottom. The right-side description indicates symptoms that occur when there is a mismatch between the explanation and each section.

data.code:
traceparent: 00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01

with tracer.start_as_current_span("chat gpt-4o") as llm_span:
    llm_span.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "chat")
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("execute_tool lookup_order") as tool_span:
        tool_span.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "execute_tool")

notes.note: The Traceparent header consists of four fields in order: version, trace-id (32 characters), parent-id (16 characters), and trace-flags. The trace-id identifies the entire request, while the parent-id refers to the originating span, becoming the parent of a new span received by the downstream service. The bit 01 in trace-flags indicates that the caller recommends sampling this trace, but it is not a mandatory rule. If the trace-id is all zeros or contains incorrect length, the receiving side will ignore the header, preventing the trace from continuing.

Include both the operation and the model name in the span name. With a name constructed this way, it becomes immediately clear in the trace list which model call is being referenced. If names are identical or ambiguous, it becomes difficult to identify slow calls.
This span indicates that it is a model conversation call via the gen_ai.operation.name attribute. If this attribute is missing, the backend might fail to interpret the span as an LLM call.

Make the tool execution span a child of the LLM call span and set the operation type to execute_tool. Since the tool execution time is distinct from the model conversation call, it becomes possible to determine whether the slowdown is due to the model or the tool.

screens.outro: Since you've learned how to read, I'll now directly work through an example where a trace is broken.

screens.title: Case Explanation: The reason trace propagation fails is context propagation.
screens.lead: The instructor walks through a case where the trace is split into two parts step by step. Select the next arrow to follow the sequence: observe, header comparison, root cause candidates, action, and verification.

visual.alt: A diagram showing side by side the process of merging two fragmented trace segments into a single trace after context propagation.

steps.title: Situation: The same request is perceived as two parts
steps.body: The traces generated by the gateway and the traces generated by the LLM call service appear to be divided into different trace IDs. Even though they originate from the same user request, we cannot link these two traces together, so we cannot determine how long the LLM phase lasts within the 9-second timeframe.

steps.title: Stage 1 Observation: root span without parents
steps.body: In the root span of an LLM service, there is no parent, and the trace ID differs from that of the gateway. This means the receiving side either did not receive parent information or received it but did not use it.

steps.title: Step 2 Header Contrast: Read the values side by side
steps.body: The trace-id from the gateway is read alongside the value received by the LLM service. If the received value is entirely absent, it indicates loss in the middle of the flow; if a value is present but its format is incorrect, the receiving side discards it. The root cause depends on which side is affected.

steps.title: Step 3: Potential Causes: Point of Loss
steps.body: A proxy that removes headers, an HTTP client without a measurement library, a segment passing through a queue where headers are lost, and malformed header values are typical candidates. Verify at which point along the request path the value disappears.

steps.title: Step 4 action direction: Propagate only at necessary points directly.
steps.body: Inject and extract context only at points where propagation does not occur, using the Propagators API. Propagation is typically handled by the monitoring library, so instead of directly managing all calls, only handle points where propagation has been interrupted.

steps.title: Step 5 Verification: Connected in a single trace
steps.body: After fixing, verify that the same request is linked as both parent and child spans under a single trace. If so, the LLM segment's duration will be visible, and you can now view the reason for the previously confusing 9-second delay segment by segment.

steps.title: Conclusion: Minimum obligations of the intermediate system
steps.body: An intermediate system must at minimum pass through traceparent and tracestate unchanged in order to prevent trace fragmentation. The lesson from this case is to first verify where the context is being lost, rather than immediately suspecting the model or code when a trace is broken.

screens.outro: We have completed the example; now I will summarize the core concepts to conclude.

screens.title: Core takeaway: Tracing requires context to be propagated to continue.
screens.lead: Let's summarize the course content in a coherent flow. Begin by reviewing the initial 9-second request scene.

paragraphs: The three signals answer different questions. Logs record individual events, metrics show aggregated numerical data over a period of time, and traces display the path a request took. To understand why a request took nine seconds, traces are required.

Tracing requires context to be propagated between services. The trace ID and span ID are carried in the W3C Trace Context's traceparent header as services communicate, and the receiving side must match the version, trace-id, parent-id, and trace-flags format to properly establish the trace. Intermediate systems must pass through both traceparent and tracestate headers unaltered.

The LLM call span includes common properties defined by the GenAI semantic contract. By specifying the operation type as gen_ai.operation.name, and recording the model name, token count, and error information, you can identify slow or expensive calls regardless of the provider used.

callout.label: Go to the beginning scene
callout.text: The average delay time graph indicates that the delay is slow, and the subsequent trace reveals that the LLM segment is the cause. The context propagation for signal transmission creates this difference.

checks.intro: The issue is reading the header directly. The result is not recorded.
checks.q:
The service that received this header did not continue the trace and instead started a new one. What part of the header should raise the most suspicion?  
traceparent: 00-00000000000000000000000000000000-b7ad6b7169203331-01
options: Version field of 00 is a value that is not supported.
Trace flags 01 forces sampling, which disconnects the connection.
parent-id is too short at 16 digits
If the trace-id is entirely zero, it is invalid and the header is ignored.
checks.explain: If the trace-id is all zeros, the side that considers it an invalid value ignores traceparent, resulting in a new trace with no parent.

wrong.0: 00 is the version value used in this format.
wrong.1: Trace flags are merely recommended for sampling and do not disable connections.
wrong.2: parent-id is a 16-digit hexadecimal number with the correct length.

glossary.def: It is the property of being able to determine why something is happening simply by observing the signals that exit the system, without needing to understand its internal workings.
This is observation output emitted by the system, similar to traces, metrics, and logs.
This is a mechanism that transfers trace ID and span ID across services to connect spans from multiple services into a single trace.
The HTTP headers defined by W3C Trace Context represent the trace context of a request in a fixed-length format.
This is an OpenTelemetry specification that unifies attribute names and meanings for LLM call spans and metrics.

misconceptions.myth: The more logs are generated, the better the observability is ensured.
misconceptions.fact: Signals must be connected in context to be able to trace their root causes. Dispersed logs across different services cannot be linked together by the same request, making sequential reading difficult.

misconceptions.myth: Just having the average delay time graph allows you to identify slow sections.
misconceptions.fact: The graph only indicates that a request is slow. The trace, which shows the request path, reveals which segment took longer.

misconceptions.myth: Context propagation always requires directly writing code.
misconceptions.fact: Radiation is typically handled by the measurement library. It can only be directly managed via the Propagators API at the point where automatic radiation has been interrupted.

misconceptions.myth: traceparent is always accepted as long as it has a value.
misconceptions.fact: Values with incorrect format or trace-id consisting entirely of zeros are ignored by the receiving side, resulting in the creation of a new trace without a parent and thereby breaking the flow.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Logs record events, metrics represent aggregated data over a period of time, and traces show the path a request takes.
The trace ID and span ID are carried in the traceparent header as services intercommunicate, and they must match so that the receiving side can properly link them.
GenAI semantic contracts provide a common name for LLM invocation properties, enabling comparison regardless of the provider.
